assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED opened a genuinely new regime: strong, controllable coupling of a single artificial atom to a single microwave photon on a chip. It provides the dispersive readout, two-qubit gating and bus architecture underlying essentially all superconducting quantum processors, and it spawned waveguide QED and microwave quantum optics. It follows naturally from last year's recognition of macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits and shows how foundational physics became an enabling platform.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 Blais-Huang-Wallraff-Girvin-Schoelkopf proposal and the Wallraff et al. Nature experiment are the decisive core. Blais (theory), Wallraff (first strong-coupling experiment) and Schoelkopf (leading the Yale group and transmon/cQED architecture) form a clean three-person configuration. Steven Girvin and others contributed to the theory and are not in the supplied credit, and I cannot propose them. I should declare close professional ties to this community.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended in many laboratories over two decades, with a stable interpretation and wide use in quantum-limited amplification, qubit readout and photon-qubit interfaces. Recognition now appears timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views cQED as sufficiently distinct from the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits.
Credit for the original theory proposal beyond the supplied names (for example Girvin) is not resolved within this candidate.
My own proximity to the field (superconducting circuits, WACQT) may bias my judgement and could call for recusal.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller 1995 proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions, and its experimental realisation, established a concrete route to controllable quantum computation. Ion platforms remain among the highest-fidelity qubit systems and have demonstrated entanglement, gates and small algorithms. Clear conceptual originality combined with sustained experimental follow-through.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the decisive theorists. Blatt led the early experimental realisations of the gate and of multi-ion entanglement. Wineland, who shares the underlying ion-control foundations, was already honoured in 2012 and Haroche's and Wineland's prize addressed single-quantum control; Blatt's credit versus other experimental groups (for example Monroe, Wineland's NIST group) is not fully settled by the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with multiple independent groups and commercial platforms, though the practical promise of scalable fault-tolerant machines is still ahead. The discovery-level contribution is secure.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for measuring and manipulating individual quantum systems.
Allocation of experimental credit between Blatt and other ion-trap groups.
Overlap with the Cirac-Zoller entry B044 and the optical-lattice entry B025.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised clean, tunable quantum many-body Hamiltonians, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition as the landmark. They enabled quantum simulation of Hubbard physics, and later single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes. A clear case of an experiment making basic quantum phenomena visible and controllable.
assessment.attribution: Zoller's theory (with Jaksch et al.) proposed the Mott transition in optical lattices, Greiner and Bloch performed the 2002 experiment and then developed the microscope work. The supplied names also include Cirac, but I use a configuration that follows the most distinctive contributions and avoids duplicating the trapped-ion candidate. Hänsch, Kasevich and others are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and broadly reproduced; quantum simulation results are now moving to regimes beyond classical simulation, though many headline claims depend on the specific platform.
uncertainties: Overlap with Zoller and Cirac in other entries and with the 2001 BEC and 2018 optical-tweezer prizes.
Whether the Mott-transition experiment or the broader simulation programme should be the prize unit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theory of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, with the 2007 HgTe experiment by Molenkamp's group, launched a whole field of topological band matter. It has had clear lasting impact, both as concept and as materials discovery. This is outside my core field, so I defer partly to colleagues in condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the theoretical foundations; Molenkamp led the first experimental demonstration. Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang proposed the HgTe mechanism and Zhang has died, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp configuration is plausible, but Bernevig-Hughes credit is not in the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed (ARPES on Bi-based 3D insulators, transport in HgTe), stable interpretation, and a decade or more of impact; recognition is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Allocation versus Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and versus the 3D topological insulator work (Moore, Balents, Fu, Hasan).
Overlap with the 2016 topological phase transitions prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum control of mechanical motion, including ground-state cooling, strong optomechanical coupling and quantum states of macroscopic oscillators, extends quantum physics to massive objects, and links closely to circuit and phononic quantum devices (including surface-acoustic-wave work I know well). It is a clean test of quantum behaviour at larger scales.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and colleagues demonstrated a mechanical resonator in its quantum ground state coupled to a qubit; Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg developed cavity optomechanics, cooling and strong coupling. The three-person configuration is reasonable but the field has many contributors (O'Connell, Painter, Lehnert, Teufel) outside the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced across platforms, but the discovery is more a collection of milestones than a single sharp result, and applications such as sensing and transduction are still developing.
uncertainties: Which milestone constitutes the prize-worthy discovery and who made it.
Overlap with the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits.
Many significant contributors are not in the credited set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction (Shor's code, Steane's code, Kitaev's toric/surface code and fault-tolerance ideas) is conceptually fundamental: it shows that quantum information can be protected in principle. I stress that full-scale error correction is the key to useful quantum processors.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane introduced the first codes; Kitaev introduced topological codes and fault-tolerant anyon ideas. The set is credible, though Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme and others also made decisive contributions.
assessment.maturity: Recent below-threshold surface-code experiments strengthen the case, but scalable logical qubits are still in progress, so the prize could be premature and the discovery is more informational than a physical phenomenon.
uncertainties: Whether Nobel criteria in physics favour this theory over experimental demonstrations.
Attribution is spread over many theorists.
Timing relative to forthcoming experimental milestones.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single-spin control and optical readout of colour centres (notably nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond) at room temperature gave a robust solid-state platform for quantum sensing, networking and small registers. Important both fundamentally and technologically.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko did the first optical detection of single NV spins; Awschalom contributed coherent control and defect spins in other materials such as SiC. Lukin is also credited and has major contributions to NV quantum registers and networks, but the maximum is three.
assessment.maturity: Well reproduced in many laboratories. Impact is broad but spread over sensing, networks and computing, so a single discovery citation is somewhat diffuse.
uncertainties: Four credited names and no clean cut; excluding Lukin is a judgement call.
Breadth of the field complicates a precise citation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84, E91) is a foundational idea linking quantum mechanics to information security, and E91 ties directly to Bell tests. Conceptually original and tied to the 2022 prize topics.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard introduced BB84, Ekert the entanglement-based protocol. A natural three-person set. Wiesner's conjugate coding is a precursor with no credit here.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally verified and commercially deployed, though the prize may depend on whether the committee regards it as a physics discovery or an information-theoretic invention, and the 2022 prize already recognised related Bell-test work.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize for entangled photons and Bell inequalities.
Whether a protocol proposal counts as a physics discovery.
